12.1: Arjuna opens with a practical question: is it better to worship you in a personal form, or meditate on the imperishable, unmanifest reality beyond all form? He wants to know which path masters yoga more fully. The traditions read this differently: Śaṅkara glosses the question as being about samādhi, absorption into the formless; Rāmānuja asks simply which practice brings deeper knowledge, without ranking the formless above the personal.
12.2: Krishna answers without hesitating: those who fix their minds on him, worship steadily, and hold supreme faith are, by his own reckoning, the most complete in yoga. He settles Arjuna's either/or with a clear preference for the personal path, even before he turns to honor the other one.
12.3: Krishna then honors that other path too. Some meditate instead on the imperishable and unmanifest — that which is everywhere, unthinkable, unchanging, constant. He doesn't dismiss it; it's a real practice with its own discipline.
12.4: Those who take this harder road restrain their senses, stay even-minded through every circumstance, and work for the good of all beings. Krishna says plainly that they, too, arrive at him in the end.
12.5: But he's honest about the cost: fixing the mind on what has no form and no image is exceptionally hard for anyone still living in a body. He isn't discouraging the formless path, only naming how demanding it really is.
12.6: By contrast, those who dedicate every action to Krishna, hold him as the highest goal, and meditate on him alone, with nothing dividing their attention, walk the surer road he's just named. Nothing else competes for their focus.
12.7: For these single-minded devotees, Krishna promises speed: he becomes their deliverer from the ocean of birth and death without delay. A mind fully turned toward him draws a swift response.
12.8: Krishna gives Arjuna the highest rung of the practical ladder first: settle your mind on me, let your intellect rest in me, and from here on you will live in me. It's the most direct instruction — full absorption, if it's within reach.
12.9: If steady absorption isn't within reach, there's a next rung: reach him instead through abhyāsa yoga, the yoga of repeated, patient practice. Effort sustained over time can do what one leap of concentration cannot.
12.10: If even disciplined practice proves too hard, Krishna offers a further rung: simply do your work for his sake. Even action alone, offered this way, brings a person to perfection.
12.11: And if that, too, is out of reach, there's one more rung, the gentlest of all: take refuge in him and simply let go of the results of whatever you do, with self-control. It's the ladder's easiest step, open to anyone.
12.12: Krishna then ranks the rungs he's just laid out: knowledge surpasses mechanical practice, meditation surpasses knowledge, and renouncing the fruits of action surpasses even meditation. Peace, he says, follows renunciation immediately — the shortest route of all.
12.13: Krishna now sketches the devotee quality by quality. He starts with the basics: hatred toward no creature, genuine friendliness and compassion, no clinging sense of 'mine' or self-importance, evenness through pleasure and pain, and a forgiving nature.
12.14: Add to that a devotee who stays content, steady in meditation, self-controlled, firm in conviction, with mind and intellect turned toward Krishna. This person, he says plainly, is dear to him.
12.15: This devotee neither disturbs the world nor is disturbed by it — free from the swings of joy, irritation, fear, and anxiety that most people live inside. That steadiness is itself, Krishna says, dear to him.
12.16: More traits follow: wanting little, inwardly clean, capable without anxiety over outcomes, untroubled, not clinging to every new undertaking. Krishna calls this devotee dear to him again, quality after quality.
12.17: Neither elated nor repelled, neither grieving nor grasping, letting go of both good and bad results alike, while staying full of devotion — this person, too, Krishna names as dear to him.
12.18: The equanimity runs deeper still: the same toward friend and enemy, in honor and disgrace, through heat and cold, pleasure and pain — and free of clinging attachment to any of it.
12.19: Unmoved by blame or praise, at ease with silence, content with whatever comes, unattached to any fixed home, steady-minded, and devoted — such a person, Krishna says, is dear to him.
12.20: Krishna closes by naming the whole picture he's drawn an 'immortal dharma,' a timeless way to live. Whoever follows it with faith, holding him as the highest goal, is exceedingly dear to him.
